./export.sh | tee export.log

explanation: nohup makes the process ignore the hangup signal sent when the session closes, and the trailing & runs it in the background so the shell is free. Running the script in the foreground, with or without output redirection or tee, ties it to the session, so it is normally killed when the connection closes. fg brings an existing background job to the foreground and does not start a script.

prompt: An engineer starts a long-running script in the background with ./sync.sh & and later needs to answer a prompt it is waiting on. The jobs command lists it as [1]. Which command brings the job back to the foreground?

options.text: bg %1
kill %1
fg %1
disown %1

explanation: fg %1 moves job 1 into the foreground so it can read input from the terminal. bg resumes a stopped job in the background, leaving it there. kill sends a signal that normally ends the job, and disown removes it from the shell's job table, so it can no longer be brought back with fg.

prompt: A team must apply the same database schema changes, in the same order, to dev, test and production, and must know exactly which changes each environment has received. Which approach meets these needs?

options.text: Versioned migration scripts applied by a tool that records which have run
Engineers running ad hoc SQL against each database from their own notes
Copying the production database over test and dev after every change
Editing the tables in a graphical tool and exporting a screenshot of the result

explanation: Migration tools apply numbered scripts in order and record which ones have run (usually in a table in the database), so every environment receives the same changes and its version is known. Ad hoc SQL from notes is not repeatable or tracked. Copying production data downward spreads sensitive data and hides which change produced which schema, and screenshots are not executable.

prompt: A deployment applies database migration 0042, which adds a column, and the new release then fails. The team wants to undo the schema change in a controlled way. What does a typical migration framework provide for this?

options.text: Automatic deletion of the database followed by an empty rebuild
A merge conflict marker inserted into the migration history table
A new source control branch that the database server switches over to
A down migration that reverses 0042 and updates the recorded version

explanation: Migration frameworks usually pair each up migration with a down migration that reverses it, and the tool updates its record of the current version after running it. Dropping and rebuilding the database destroys data. Merge conflict markers are a source control artifact, not a database feature, and a database does not switch branches.

prompt: Developers want every pull request to get its own complete test environment that is created automatically, used for review, and destroyed when the pull request is merged or closed. What is this type of environment called?

options.text: An ephemeral environment
A persistent environment
A disaster recovery environment
A golden image environment

explanation: An ephemeral environment is short-lived, created on demand from code for a specific purpose and torn down afterward, which matches a per-pull-request preview. A persistent environment is long-lived, such as production or shared staging. Disaster recovery environments stand by for failover, and a golden image is a base machine image rather than an environment lifecycle.

prompt: A team is deciding how to manage its customer database, which must keep its data across every release and must be backed up and changed only through controlled migrations. How should this environment be treated?

options.text: As an ephemeral environment that is rebuilt from scratch for every pull request
As a persistent environment that is updated in place under change control
As a throwaway environment deleted at the end of each working day
As a local environment that each developer copies to a laptop

explanation: A persistent environment lives for a long time and keeps its state, so it is changed carefully through migrations and protected by backups. Rebuilding it for every pull request or deleting it daily would destroy customer data. Copying a customer database to laptops creates data protection problems and does not manage the shared environment.

prompt: An engineer must perform a one-time correction: rename 300 files in a specific order, call an API after each rename, and stop at the first failure. No ongoing desired state needs to be maintained. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: A declarative template that describes the final set of resources
A pull-based agent that enforces the file names every 30 minutes
An imperative script that performs each step in sequence
A load balancer rule that redirects requests to the new file names

explanation: One-off, ordered tasks with step-by-step control flow suit imperative script writing, where the author decides exactly what runs and when to stop. Declarative templates describe ongoing desired state and leave ordering to the tool. A pull-based agent continuously enforces state, which is unnecessary for a one-time job, and a load balancer rule does not rename files.

prompt: A team wants to write only the end state of its infrastructure, such as three web servers behind one load balancer, and have the tool work out which create, update or delete actions are needed on each run. Which approach should they use?

options.text: A declarative tool such as Terraform
An imperative Bash script of CLI calls
A sequence of manual console changes
A cron job that runs create commands

explanation: Declarative tools compare the described state with the real state and calculate the actions needed, so the author does not script each step. An imperative script runs the exact commands written, in order, and must handle existing resources itself. Manual console changes are not code at all, and a cron job running create commands repeats the creation on every run.

prompt: A security patch to a configuration file must reach 40 servers immediately, at a moment chosen by the operator, with results reported back in the same session. Which provisioning technique fits best?

options.text: Pull, where each server checks the configuration server on its next scheduled run
Golden image rebuild scheduled for the next quarterly maintenance window
Push, where a control node connects out and applies the change on demand
Manual change made by each server owner when the patch notice is read

explanation: In the push model, the control node starts the run and contacts the servers, so the change happens when the operator decides and results return immediately. In the pull model, servers apply changes on their own schedule, so timing depends on their next check-in. A quarterly rebuild is far too slow, and manual changes by each owner are unreliable and not reported centrally.

prompt: An organisation runs thousands of short-lived, auto-scaled instances that appear and disappear without notice. Each new instance must configure itself as soon as it boots, without a central system needing to know it exists. Which provisioning technique fits best?

options.text: Push, where an operator adds each instance to an inventory and starts a run
Pull, where each instance fetches and applies its own configuration
Manual setup, where an engineer logs in to each instance after it launches
Push, where the control node scans the subnet hourly for new instances

explanation: In the pull model, each node contacts the configuration source itself at boot and on a schedule, so new instances configure themselves with no central inventory update. Push requires the controller to know about each target, which is hard when instances come and go constantly, and an hourly scan leaves new instances unconfigured for up to an hour. Manual setup cannot keep up with auto-scaling.

prompt: Whenever a file is uploaded to a cloud storage bucket, a thumbnail must be generated within seconds. The team does not want a server polling the bucket. Which design fits best?

options.text: Run a virtual machine that lists the bucket contents every hour
Ask users to email the operations team after each upload
Schedule a nightly batch job that processes all files uploaded that day
Use bucket event notifications to invoke a function per new object

explanation: Storage event notifications fire as soon as an object is created and can invoke a function directly, so processing starts within seconds with no polling. Hourly listing and nightly batches add long delays and waste resources between runs. Relying on users to email operations is manual and unreliable.

prompt: An order service produces bursts of requests that the downstream billing service cannot always process immediately. Orders must not be lost if billing is slow or briefly offline, and failed items must be retried. What should be placed between the two services?

options.text: A message queue that buffers orders until billing consumes them
A DNS record with a low TTL that points to the billing service
A cron job that calls the billing service once every night with the day's orders
A load balancer health check that marks billing as healthy

explanation: A message queue decouples producers from consumers, holds messages durably until they are processed and supports retries (often with a dead-letter queue for repeated failures). DNS only resolves names and does not store requests. A nightly cron job adds a long delay, and a health check does not store or retry orders when billing is unavailable.

prompt: A team is considering function as a service (FaaS) for several workloads. Which workload is the best fit?

options.text: A database server that must keep large amounts of data in memory for weeks
A batch job that runs continuously for eight hours on dedicated hardware
A short handler that resizes an image whenever an upload event occurs
A legacy desktop application that requires a graphical user interface

explanation: FaaS runs short, stateless code in response to events, scales automatically and charges per execution, which suits an event-driven image resize. Platforms impose execution time limits and do not keep in-memory state between invocations, so a long-lived database server and an eight-hour batch job are poor fits. A graphical desktop application cannot run as a function.

prompt: When a new user account is created, three independent systems must react: the email service sends a welcome message, the billing system creates a customer record and the audit system logs the event. Each must receive every event. Which pattern fits best?

options.text: Send the event to a single queue that the three services compete to read
Publish the event to a topic that all three services subscribe to
Have the account service call each system in turn and wait for each reply
Write the event to a log file that each system checks once a day

explanation: A publish/subscribe topic delivers a copy of each event to every subscriber, so all three services receive it independently. With one shared queue, consumers compete and each message is processed by only one of them. Sequential calls couple the account service to all three systems and fail if one is down, and a daily log check is slow and fragile.

prompt:
An automation script sends the following request and receives the response shown.

curl -X POST https://api.example.com/v1/servers \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "web03", "size": "small"}'

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: /v1/servers/317

What does the response indicate?

options.text: The request was accepted but the server will create the resource later
The request was redirected and must be sent again to /v1/servers/317
The resource already existed, so server 317 was updated in place
A new server resource was created and can be read at /v1/servers/317

explanation: 201 Created means the request created a new resource, and the Location header gives its URI. Deferred processing is signalled by 202 Accepted. A redirect uses a 3xx status code, and a successful update of an existing resource normally returns 200 OK or 204 No Content.

prompt:
A script creates a record with the following command and receives HTTP/1.1 415 Unsupported Media Type.

curl -X POST https://api.example.com/v1/users -d '{"name": "svc-backup"}'

The JSON body is valid. What should be changed?

options.text: Change -X POST to -X GET so that the body is read correctly
Add -H "Content-Type: application/json" to the command
Add -L so that curl follows the server's redirect response
Replace the single quotes with double quotes around the body

explanation: With -d, curl sends the body as application/x-www-form-urlencoded unless told otherwise, so the API rejects it with 415; setting the Content-Type header to application/json fixes this. GET requests are for reading and do not create records. -L follows 3xx redirects, which this response is not, and the quoting style does not change the media type.

prompt: An API stores server objects with name, size, owner and description fields. A script must change only the description of server 42 and leave every other field unchanged, sending only the new description. Which method is designed for this?

options.text: PATCH
PUT
POST
GET

explanation: PATCH applies a partial modification to an existing resource, so sending only the description changes just that field. PUT replaces the entire state of the target resource with the representation sent. POST is generally used to create a new resource or trigger processing, and GET only reads data.

prompt: An engineer sends PUT /v1/servers/42 with the body {"description": "db replica"}. Afterward, a GET request shows that the server's owner and size fields are now empty. What explains this?

options.text: PUT is not idempotent, so the request was applied more than once
The server returned a 3xx code that silently cleared the other fields
The GET request returned a cached copy from before the PUT was sent
PUT replaces the whole resource with the representation that was sent

explanation: PUT asks the server to replace the target resource's state with the enclosed representation, so fields left out of the body can be removed or reset; PATCH should be used for partial updates. PUT is defined as idempotent. A 3xx response is a redirect and does not modify data, and a stale cached copy would show the old values, not empty ones.

prompt: A cleanup script runs curl -i -X DELETE https://api.example.com/v1/snapshots/88 and receives HTTP/1.1 204 No Content with an empty body. How should the script interpret this?

options.text: The snapshot does not exist, so the deletion was not performed
The request failed because the response body is unexpectedly empty
The deletion succeeded and the server has no content to return
The deletion is queued and must be confirmed with a second request

explanation: 204 No Content is a success code meaning the request was fulfilled and there is no response body, which is common for DELETE. A missing snapshot is reported with 404 Not Found. An empty body is expected with 204, not an error, and a queued operation would normally return 202 Accepted.

prompt: A client library automatically retries requests after network timeouts. The team wants to know which requests can be repeated safely because sending them twice has the same effect on the server as sending them once. Which two methods are defined as idempotent by HTTP semantics? (Choose two.)

options.text: PUT
DELETE
POST
PATCH

explanation: HTTP defines PUT and DELETE (along with GET, HEAD and OPTIONS) as idempotent: repeating a PUT stores the same state, and repeating a DELETE leaves the resource deleted. POST is not idempotent, because repeating it can create duplicate resources. PATCH is not guaranteed to be idempotent, because a patch such as 'append an item' changes the result each time it is applied.

prompt: An API can return data as JSON or XML. A script needs JSON and must tell the server which format it wants in the response. Which request header should the script send?

options.text: Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json
Content-Length: application/json
Authorization: application/json

explanation: The Accept header tells the server which media types the client can handle in the response, so the server can return JSON. Content-Type describes the body the client is sending, not the format it wants back. Content-Length gives the body size in bytes, and Authorization carries credentials.

prompt: A script has obtained an OAuth 2.0 access token in the variable TOKEN and must call a protected API with it. Which curl option sends the token correctly?

options.text: -H "Accept: Bearer $TOKEN"
--data-urlencode "access_token=$TOKEN" -X GET
-u "$TOKEN:Bearer"
-H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

explanation: Bearer tokens are sent in the Authorization header using the Bearer scheme. The Accept header lists response media types and is not read as credentials. Sending the token as a form-body parameter is only an optional fallback in the bearer token standard and must not be used with GET, and -u sends HTTP Basic authentication with a user name and password.

prompt: A nightly job that has worked for weeks starts failing with HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized and the header WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token". No code has changed. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The access token has expired or been revoked and must be renewed
The account is authenticated but lacks permission for the resource
The API endpoint has moved permanently to a new URL
The API server crashed while it was processing the request

explanation: 401 means the request lacks valid authentication credentials, and invalid_token points to an expired or revoked token, so the job must obtain a new one. An authenticated client without permission receives 403 Forbidden. A permanent move is signalled by 301 or 308, and a server crash produces a 5xx code.

prompt: A service account's token is valid, and the same token reads data successfully. When the script sends DELETE /v1/projects/9 with it, the API returns 403 Forbidden. What should the engineer do?

options.text: Request a new token, because the existing token has expired overnight
Change DELETE to POST because the API does not support DELETE
Grant the service account a role that allows deleting projects
Wait and retry because the server is temporarily overloaded

explanation: 403 Forbidden means the server understood who the caller is but refuses the action, so the account needs a role or scope that allows the deletion. An expired token would cause 401, and reads with the same token are working. An unsupported method returns 405 Method Not Allowed, and overload is reported with 503 or 429.

prompt: A script sends GET https://api.example.com/v1/sever/12 and receives 404 Not Found. Other endpoints on the same API work with the same token. What should the engineer check first?

options.text: Whether the API server has run out of memory
Whether the token has expired and needs renewal
Whether the URL path is spelled correctly
Whether the request body has the correct content type

explanation: 404 means the server found nothing at the requested URI, and the path here contains the typo sever instead of server (or the ID may not exist). Memory exhaustion causes a 5xx error. An expired token produces 401, and a GET request has no body whose content type could cause a 404.

prompt:
A bulk import script receives the following response after sending 200 requests in a few seconds.

HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 30

What should the script do?

options.text: Retry the same request immediately in a tight loop until it succeeds
Pause for at least 30 seconds, then continue at a lower request rate
Switch from HTTPS to HTTP so that the rate limit no longer applies
Treat the error as permanent and delete the records already imported

explanation: 429 means the client has exceeded a rate limit, and Retry-After says how long to wait, so the script should wait and then slow down, ideally with exponential backoff. Retrying immediately makes the throttling worse. Switching protocols does not bypass rate limits and weakens security, and the error is temporary, so the imported records are still valid.

prompt: A script runs curl -s http://api.example.com/v1/status and receives an empty body. With -i, the output starts with HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently and Location: https://api.example.com/v1/status. Which change makes curl retrieve the status automatically?

options.text: Add the -I option so curl sends a HEAD request
Add the -f option so curl fails on HTTP errors
Add the -o option so the body is saved to a file
Add the -L option so curl follows the redirect

explanation: curl does not follow redirects by default, and -L makes it repeat the request at the URL in the Location header. -I sends HEAD, which returns only headers. -f changes how HTTP error codes of 400 and above are reported and has no effect on a 301, and -o only changes where the (empty) body is written.

prompt: A monitoring client sends a GET request for a large configuration document with the header If-None-Match: "a7f3", which is the ETag it received last time. The server replies with 304 Not Modified and no body. What should the client do?

options.text: Use its cached copy, because the document has not changed
Request the document again without the If-None-Match header
Treat the document as deleted and remove it from the cache
Report an error, because a GET response must always have a body

explanation: 304 Not Modified answers a conditional request: the resource still matches the ETag, so the client's cached copy is current. Requesting again without the header just downloads the same unchanged content. A deleted resource would return 404 or 410, and 304 responses are defined to have no body.

prompt: An API gateway sits in front of an application server. Clients suddenly receive HTTP/1.1 502 Bad Gateway, even for requests that worked earlier. Where should troubleshooting start?

options.text: With the client's request syntax and JSON payload format
With the upstream application server behind the gateway
With the client's access token and its permission scopes
With the redirect rules that send clients to a new URL

explanation: 502 Bad Gateway means the gateway or proxy received an invalid response, or none, from the upstream server it forwards to, so the upstream application is the likely problem. Request syntax problems return 400, and token or permission problems return 401 or 403. Redirects use 3xx codes, not 502.

prompt: A deployment script must download a release archive from https://repo.example.com/app-2.4.1.tar.gz and save it to disk. Running curl https://repo.example.com/app-2.4.1.tar.gz printed unreadable binary data to the terminal. Which command saves the file correctly?

options.text: curl -I https://repo.example.com/app-2.4.1.tar.gz > app.tar.gz
curl -X DELETE https://repo.example.com/app-2.4.1.tar.gz
wget --spider https://repo.example.com/app-2.4.1.tar.gz
wget -O app.tar.gz https://repo.example.com/app-2.4.1.tar.gz

explanation: wget is designed for non-interactive downloads and -O writes the content to the named file (curl -o would also work). By default curl writes the body to standard output, and with -I it fetches only the headers, so the file would contain headers instead of the archive. -X DELETE asks the server to delete the archive, and --spider checks that the file exists without downloading it.

prompt: A team builds API test requests in a graphical client, shares them, and switches between dev and prod base URLs with variables. They now want the same tests to run automatically in the CI pipeline. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Postman collections and environments, run in CI with Newman
wget commands typed by hand during each pipeline run
A spreadsheet that lists each endpoint and its expected status
Browser bookmarks for each API endpoint shared with the team

explanation: Postman organises requests and their tests in collections, stores per-environment values such as base URLs in environments, and its command-line runner Newman executes collections in CI. Typing wget commands by hand is not automation. A spreadsheet documents tests but cannot run them, and bookmarks can only send simple GET requests with no assertions.

prompt: A pipeline step runs curl -s -o result.json https://api.example.com/v1/report. When the API returns 500 Internal Server Error, the step still passes and later steps fail on a bad file. Which change makes the step fail on HTTP error responses?

options.text: Add the -v option so curl prints more detail about the request
Add the -k option so curl skips verification of the certificate
Add the -f (--fail) option so curl exits non-zero on HTTP errors
Remove the -s option so curl shows its progress meter in the log

explanation: By default curl exits with status 0 whenever it receives any HTTP response, even an error; with -f it returns a non-zero exit code (22) for responses of 400 and above, so the pipeline step fails. -v and removing -s add output but do not change the exit code. -k disables certificate verification, which weakens security and is unrelated to the 500 error.

prompt:
A pipeline step that calls an internal API fails with the following output.

curl: (6) Could not resolve host: inventory.corp.example

The same command works from an engineer's workstation on the office network. What should be investigated first?

options.text: Whether the API token used by the pipeline has expired
Whether the CI runner can resolve the internal DNS name
Whether the API's TLS certificate has been renewed
Whether the JSON request body has a trailing comma

explanation: curl error 6 means the host name could not be resolved to an address, so the runner's DNS configuration (for example, no access to the internal DNS zone) is the first thing to check. An expired token would produce a 401 response, which requires a successful connection first. Certificate problems are reported as SSL errors after the name resolves, and a malformed body would be rejected by the server with a 4xx code.

prompt: An API call from a new CI runner hangs and times out after 30 seconds without any HTTP response. The same call from another subnet returns 200 within milliseconds, and DNS resolves correctly on the runner. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The API returned 503 Service Unavailable because it is overloaded
The runner's access token lacks the scope needed to call the API
A firewall or security group is dropping the runner's traffic
The response body is not valid JSON, so curl waits for more data

explanation: A connection that hangs until a timeout, while other networks connect instantly, typically means packets are being dropped by a firewall rule, security group or ACL on the path. A 503 is an HTTP response, which the runner never receives. A missing scope would produce 403, also an HTTP response, and curl does not wait for a body to be valid JSON.

prompt: After a network change, configuration agents on servers in one subnet stop checking in with the configuration server. The agent service is running on each server, and agents in other subnets are unaffected. Which action should be taken first?

options.text: Reinstall the agent package on every server in the affected subnet
Rewrite the configuration code in a declarative language
Increase the agent's run interval so it checks in less often
Confirm the subnet can still reach the configuration server's port

explanation: Agents that are running but cannot check in after a network change point to a connectivity problem, so test that the subnet can reach the server's listening port (for example with nc or a firewall log check). Reinstalling the agent does not fix a blocked path. The style of the configuration code has nothing to do with connectivity, and a longer interval only delays the failed check-ins.

options.text: web07 is down or a firewall is blocking SSH to it
The playbook has a YAML indentation error on line 22
The SSH key was rejected with Permission denied (publickey)
A task on web07 failed because a package was not found

explanation: A connection timeout on port 22 means no SSH response arrived, which points to a host that is off or a network path or firewall blocking the port. A YAML error would stop the whole play before any host connected. A rejected key produces a Permission denied message after the connection succeeds, and a failed task is reported as FAILED, not UNREACHABLE.

prompt:
After a configuration change, an application service fails to start. Its log contains the following.

listen tcp 0.0.0.0:8080: bind: address already in use

What should the engineer do next?

options.text: Renew the TLS certificate that the application uses on port 8080
Add a DNS record for the application server's host name
Change the application's log level from INFO to DEBUG
Find the process holding port 8080, for example with ss -ltnp

explanation: The error means another process is already listening on port 8080, so the next step is to identify it (ss -ltnp or lsof) and stop it or move one of the services to a different port. TLS certificates are not involved in binding a port. DNS records affect how clients find the server, not whether the service can listen, and a more verbose log level does not free the port.

prompt: A containerised service keeps restarting. The container status shows that it exited with code 137, and the logs end abruptly with no application error. Which cause is most likely?

options.text: It was killed with SIGKILL, often for exceeding its memory limit
The application raised a Python syntax error during startup
The image could not be pulled because the registry was unreachable
The health check endpoint returned 301 instead of 200

explanation: Exit code 137 is 128 + 9, meaning the process received SIGKILL, and an out-of-memory kill for exceeding the container's memory limit is the most common reason; the container's state usually confirms it. A syntax error would appear in the logs with a normal non-zero exit code such as 1. A failed image pull means the container never starts, and a 301 health check result would not make the process exit with 137 on its own.

prompt:
An automation job that calls a partner API starts failing on a Monday with the following.

curl: (60) SSL certificate problem: certificate has expired

Nothing changed on the client side. What is the correct resolution?

options.text: Add the -k option to the curl command so validation is skipped
Change the request from HTTPS to HTTP to avoid the certificate
The partner must install a renewed certificate on the API
Set the client's system clock back to before the expiry date

explanation: The server's certificate is past its validity period, so the fix is for the API owner to install a renewed certificate. -k and switching to plain HTTP remove the protection against interception, which is unacceptable for a production integration. Changing the client clock is a fragile workaround that breaks other certificate checks and logging.

prompt:
A script connects to https://api.example.com and fails with the following.

curl: (60) SSL: no alternative certificate subject name matches target host name 'api.example.com'

The certificate is valid and was issued for www.example.com only. What should be done?

options.text: Import the certificate authority's root certificate into the client trust store
Reissue the certificate with api.example.com in its subject alternative names
Restart the API server so that the certificate is loaded again
Shorten the certificate's validity period to 90 days and reinstall it

explanation: Clients match the host name in the URL against the certificate's subject alternative names, so the certificate must include api.example.com (or a suitable wildcard). The CA is already trusted, since the error is about the name, not the issuer. Restarting reloads the same mismatched certificate, and the validity period does not affect name matching.

prompt: A new internal service uses a certificate issued by the company's private certificate authority. Calls from build agents fail with SSL certificate problem: unable to get local issuer certificate. Browsers on managed laptops work. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Add the private CA's root certificate to the build agents' trust store
Disable certificate verification in every build script that calls the service
Replace the certificate with a self-signed one generated on the server
Change the service port from 443 to 8443 so verification is not performed

explanation: The agents do not trust the private CA that signed the certificate (managed laptops already have it), so installing the CA's root certificate in the agents' trust store lets the chain be verified. Disabling verification hides the problem and allows interception. A self-signed certificate would fail the same trust check, and TLS verification does not depend on the port number.

prompt:
An application fails at startup with MissingSectionHeaderError: File contains no section headers while reading this INI file.

db_host = 10.0.2.15
[database]
port = 5432
user = app

What is the fix?

options.text: Wrap the value 10.0.2.15 in double quotes so it is read as a string
Replace each equals sign with a colon followed by a space
Indent the port and user lines so they belong to the section
Move the db_host line below the [database] section header

explanation: INI parsers such as Python's configparser expect every key to belong to a section, so a key that appears before the first [section] header triggers this error; moving it under [database] fixes it. Quoting the value does not create a section. Both = and : are accepted as delimiters by configparser, and in INI files indentation does not assign keys to sections; indented lines are treated as continuations of the previous value.

prompt:
A Compose file fails to load with the error mapping values are not allowed here, pointing at line 4.

services:
  web:
    image: nginx
     ports:
      - "80:80"

What is wrong?

options.text: The port mapping "80:80" must not be quoted because YAML numbers cannot be strings
The list item under ports must use an asterisk instead of a hyphen
ports is over-indented, so YAML reads it as part of the image value
The services key must be written in uppercase for the file to be valid

explanation: Keys at the same level must have the same indentation; the extra space makes YAML treat ports: as a continuation of the scalar nginx, and a colon there is not allowed, so ports should line up with image. Quoting "80:80" is recommended so it stays a string. YAML sequences use hyphens, not asterisks, and keys are case-sensitive but have no uppercase requirement.

prompt:
A CI pipeline file contains the following step, and the parser reports mapping values are not allowed here on that line.

steps:
  - run: echo Status: ok

Which change fixes the error while keeping the same command?

options.text: Remove the space after the first colon: run:echo Status: ok
Quote the value: run: "echo Status: ok"
Replace the hyphen with a tab character before run
Change the key to RUN in uppercase letters

explanation: An unquoted plain scalar cannot contain a colon followed by a space, because YAML reads it as another key-value separator; quoting the whole value makes it a single string. Removing the space after run: stops run from being parsed as a key at all. Tabs are not allowed for YAML indentation, and changing the key's case does not affect the colon in the value.

options.text: Put quotes around 8080, because JSON values must always be strings
Remove the comma after 8080; JSON forbids trailing commas
Replace the double quotes with single quotes around each key
Add a comment line that describes the purpose of each key

explanation: JSON forbids a comma after the last member of an object or array, so the trailing comma after 8080 makes the document invalid. Numbers are valid JSON values without quotes. JSON requires double quotes for keys and strings, so single quotes would make it worse, and JSON does not support comments.

prompt: A pipeline needs a database password to run integration tests. Today the password is written in plain text in the pipeline YAML file in the repository. What is the best replacement?

options.text: Store it in an encrypted secrets vault and fetch it at run time
Move it into a .env file that is committed next to the pipeline file
Encode it with Base64 in the YAML file so it is no longer readable
Put it in the commit message so that it is not in the code itself

explanation: An encrypted secrets vault keeps the password out of source control, controls and audits who can read it, and supplies it to the job only when it runs. A committed .env file is still plain text in the repository. Base64 is an encoding that anyone can reverse, and commit messages are part of the repository history, so the secret would still be exposed.

prompt: A deploy token for a production artifact registry was accidentally printed in a public build log. What should the team do first?

options.text: Delete the build log and keep the token
Make the repository private and keep the token in place
Revoke the token at its issuer immediately
Change the token's description to mark it as compromised

explanation: Once a credential is exposed, revoking it at the issuer immediately stops anyone from using it, and a replacement can then be issued. Deleting the log does not help anyone who already copied the token. Making the repository private does not invalidate a token that is already public, and editing its description has no effect on whether it works.

prompt: A security team wants pipeline jobs to receive database credentials that stop working automatically shortly after the job finishes, even if the job forgets to clean up. Which secrets management feature provides this?

options.text: A single static password shared by every pipeline in the organisation
A password stored in a CI variable that is changed once a year
A credentials file copied into the container image at build time
Leased credentials with a short time-to-live that expire on their own

explanation: With lease management, a secrets engine issues credentials with a time-to-live, and when the lease expires the credentials are revoked automatically. A shared static password never expires and is reused everywhere. An annual change leaves credentials valid for months, and credentials baked into an image last as long as the image and spread wherever it is copied.

prompt: A data migration job runs for about three hours, but the dynamic credentials it receives have a one-hour lease. The secrets platform allows leases to be renewed up to a maximum of eight hours. What should the job do?

options.text: Request a static credential with no expiry for long-running jobs
Renew the lease before it expires, within the maximum TTL
Store the credential in a file and reuse it after the lease ends
Split the job so each part ignores lease expiry errors

explanation: Renewing a lease before it expires extends the credential's validity, up to the maximum allowed by policy, which keeps the job working without long-lived secrets. A static credential with no expiry gives up the protection that leases provide. Once a lease expires the credential is revoked, so reusing it fails, and ignoring the resulting errors does not restore access.

prompt: A team needs realistic payment records in a test environment. Card numbers must never be stored there, but each test record must map back to its original value through a protected service when authorised. Which technique fits best?

options.text: Base64 encoding of each card number before loading it into the test database
Copying production data directly into the test environment for realism
Tokenization, replacing each card number with a token held in a secure vault
Deleting the card number column so that the records cannot be linked

explanation: Tokenization substitutes sensitive values with tokens that have no exploitable meaning, while the mapping stays in a protected token vault that authorised systems can query. Base64 is trivially reversible, so the card numbers would effectively be stored in test. Copying production data exposes it directly, and deleting the column loses the ability to map records back.

prompt: A company's CI runners sit inside the corporate network and currently have broad, permanent access to every internal system because they are considered trusted. The security team wants to apply Zero Trust principles. Which change aligns best?

options.text: Authenticate every job and grant short-lived, least-privilege access
Move the runners to a different subnet that is also inside the corporate network
Allow the runners full access only during business hours on weekdays
Give every developer the same broad access the runners have so access is consistent

explanation: Zero Trust removes implicit trust based on network location: every request is authenticated and authorised, with least privilege and short-lived credentials. Moving runners to another internal subnet keeps location-based trust. Time-of-day limits still grant broad access, and extending that access to everyone is the opposite of least privilege.

prompt: An application's database password must be changed every 30 days. Today each change requires editing configuration and redeploying every service. Which approach removes the redeployment step?

options.text: Write the new password into each service's source code and rebuild all images
Extend the rotation period to 365 days so that redeployments are rare
Store the password in the container image so that it changes with each build
Rotate it in the vault and have services read the current value at run time

explanation: With dynamic rotation, the vault changes the secret on schedule and applications fetch the current value when they need it, so no redeploy is required. Putting the password in source code or in images still forces rebuilds and exposes the secret. Extending the rotation period weakens security instead of solving the operational problem.

prompt: A team is replacing one shared database account used by all pipelines with dynamic secrets generated on demand. What is a key security benefit of this change?

options.text: The credentials never expire, so jobs no longer fail when passwords change
Each job gets unique credentials that can be traced and revoked
Every pipeline can now use the database administrator account safely
The credentials can be stored in the repository because they are random

explanation: Dynamic secrets are created per consumer when requested and expire with their lease, so each job's access is individually auditable and revocable and a leak affects only one job. They are designed to expire, not to last forever. They do not justify broader privileges, and any credential, random or not, must stay out of source control.

prompt: An investigation finds that one compromised pipeline role obtained dozens of dynamic database credentials over the past day. All of them were issued under leases by the secrets platform. What is the fastest way to cut off this access?

options.text: Revoke all leases issued to that role at once
Wait for the leases to expire on their own
Change the description of the role so that no new credentials are issued
Ask the database administrator to search the logs for each user name

explanation: Because the platform tracks every credential it issued as a lease, revoking the leases for that role or path invalidates all of them immediately. Waiting for expiry leaves the attacker with access until each lease runs out. A description change does not stop issuance or revoke anything, and searching logs by hand is slow and leaves the credentials active.

prompt: A team builds a container image in CI, then rebuilds it separately for staging and again for production. Production occasionally behaves differently from what was tested. Which practice fixes this?

options.text: Rebuild the image in each environment using the newest base image
Build the image locally on each server
Tag every image as latest so that each environment pulls the same name
Build once, store it in a registry, and promote that image

explanation: Building a single artifact and storing it in a registry means the exact tested bits are promoted through each environment. Rebuilding per environment, or on each server, can pick up different dependencies or base images. The latest tag is a moving pointer, so different environments can pull different images under the same name.

prompt: An artifact registry stores release packages. The build pipeline must publish packages, deployment jobs must download them, and nobody else should change them. Which authorization setup follows least privilege?

options.text: Administrator access for every pipeline identity so that jobs never fail
Anonymous read and write access for everyone
Write for the build identity and read-only for deploy jobs
Write access for deploy jobs and read-only access for the build pipeline

explanation: Least privilege gives each identity only what it needs: the build pipeline publishes, so it needs write access, and deploy jobs only download, so they get read-only access. Administrator access for all pipelines allows deletion or tampering. Anonymous write lets anyone replace packages, and reversing the permissions stops the build from publishing.

prompt: A pipeline logs in to the company's container registry using a senior engineer's personal user name and password. The engineer is leaving the company next week. How should registry authentication be set up?

options.text: Keep using the engineer's account and change its password after they leave
Allow anonymous pushes from the CI runner's IP address range
Use a dedicated service account or robot token stored as a CI secret
Share another engineer's personal credentials with the pipeline

explanation: A service account or robot token belongs to the automation rather than a person, can be scoped to the needed repositories and rotated without affecting people. Keeping a departed employee's account active is a security risk and the pipeline breaks when it is disabled. Anonymous pushes remove authentication, and moving to another person's credentials repeats the problem.

prompt: Production deployments reference the image app:latest. During an incident, nobody can tell which build is running or roll back to a known version. Which artifact versioning practice should the team adopt?

options.text: Keep using latest but push images only on Fridays so changes are easier to track
Tag each image with its semantic version and commit SHA, and deploy that tag
Delete older images from the registry so that only one version exists at a time
Name each image after the engineer who built it and the day of the week

explanation: Unique version tags such as 2.4.1 plus the commit SHA identify exactly which code is running and let the team redeploy an earlier version. latest is a moving pointer that hides which build is deployed, whatever the schedule. Deleting old images removes rollback targets, and names based on people and weekdays repeat and say nothing about the code.

prompt: A developer pushed a rebuilt image under the existing tag 3.2.0, replacing the image that QA had tested. The team wants the registry to stop this from ever happening again. What should be enabled?

options.text: Anonymous pull access, so testers can download any image they need
Automatic deletion of images older than seven days
A webhook that posts a chat message on each push
Tag immutability, so an existing tag cannot be overwritten

explanation: Immutable tags prevent a published tag from being pushed again with different content, so 3.2.0 always refers to the tested image. Anonymous pull access only affects who can download. Age-based deletion removes old images but does not block overwrites, and a chat notification reports the overwrite after it happens rather than preventing it.

prompt: A deployment manifest must guarantee that exactly the image content that passed security review is deployed, even if someone later moves tags in the registry. How should the image be referenced?

options.text: By its content digest, such as app@sha256:4f1c...
By the mutable tag app:stable used by the team
By the registry host name without any tag
By the build date written in the image description

explanation: A digest is a hash of the image content, so referencing it pins the exact bytes and cannot be redirected by moving a tag. A mutable tag such as stable can be repointed to different content. Omitting the tag usually resolves to latest, and a description field is not an identifier that a runtime can pull.

prompt: Builds fail several times a month when a public package index is slow or rate-limits the company. The security team also wants every third-party package scanned before use. What should the team set up?

options.text: A script that downloads every public package nightly to each developer's laptop
Direct access from each build agent to the public index with retries disabled
An internal repository manager that proxies and caches the public repositories
A rule that developers copy package source code into each project manually

explanation: A repository manager acting as a proxy for external repositories caches packages locally, so builds keep working during upstream problems, and gives a single point to scan and approve packages. Mirroring everything to laptops does not serve build agents or centralise scanning. Direct access keeps the outage and rate-limit problem, and vendoring source code by hand is error-prone and hard to update.

prompt: A critical vulnerability is announced in a widely used logging library. The security team must find out within an hour which of the company's 400 released artifacts include the affected versions. Which practice makes this possible?

options.text: Requiring developers to remember which libraries each project uses
Running a load test against each production service after the announcement
Storing every artifact under the latest tag so that there is only one to check
Generating a software bill of materials for every artifact at build time

explanation: An SBOM lists the components and versions inside each artifact, in formats such as SPDX or CycloneDX, so affected artifacts can be found by searching the SBOMs. Developer memory is incomplete and slow. Load testing measures performance, not composition, and collapsing everything to one latest tag hides which versions are deployed.

prompt: A team wants the software bill of materials (SBOM) for each release to describe exactly what shipped. When should the SBOM be produced and where should it be kept?

options.text: During each artifact build, stored with that artifact
Once a year for the whole company, stored in a shared spreadsheet
After a vulnerability is announced, from main
Before any code is written, based on the libraries the team plans to use

explanation: Generating the SBOM in the build pipeline captures the components that actually went into that artifact version, and storing it with the artifact keeps them linked. An annual company-wide list quickly goes stale. Generating from main after an announcement describes the current code, not what was released, and a plan written before coding does not reflect the final dependencies.

prompt: Developers run a long sequence of commands to lint, test and package a project, and the CI pipeline repeats the same steps with slightly different commands. Results differ between laptops and CI. Which approach makes them consistent?

options.text: Write the commands in the project wiki and ask developers to copy them carefully
Define the steps as task runner targets and call them in both places
Run the steps in CI only and stop developers from running them on laptops
Give each developer their own slightly different script so they can work faster

explanation: A task runner such as Make or a package manager's script section defines each step once under a name like test or package, so developers and CI run identical commands. Copying commands from a wiki invites drift. Blocking local runs slows feedback without fixing consistency, and per-developer scripts make the differences worse.

prompt: Integration tests need a database and a message broker. Developers currently install these by hand, and versions differ between machines. The team wants one task runner command that prepares the test environment before tests and removes it afterward. What should the task do?

options.text: Connect the tests to the production database so that every developer uses the same data
Print manual install instructions for developers
Skip the integration tests whenever the dependencies are not already installed
Start pinned dependency containers, run the tests, then remove them

explanation: Having the task provision pinned dependency containers, run the tests and clean up gives every run the same fresh environment. Testing against production risks real data and customer impact. Printed instructions keep the manual, inconsistent setup, and skipping tests hides problems instead of providing an environment.

prompt: Pipeline jobs share one long-lived test database, and tests sometimes fail because an earlier job left behind data. What is the best way to provision the environment?

options.text: Run all pipeline jobs at night so that fewer tests overlap in the shared database
Ask developers to clean up the shared database by hand after each failed run
Create a fresh database per job from code and remove it afterward
Disable the tests that fail intermittently

explanation: Provisioning an isolated environment per job from code, and tearing it down afterward, gives every test run a known clean state and removes interference between jobs. Night-time runs reduce overlap but still share state. Manual cleanup is unreliable, and disabling tests hides real problems.

prompt: A deploy script is called as ./deploy.sh --db-password "$DB_PASS". A security review flags this, even though DB_PASS comes from a vault. What is the concern?

options.text: Other users can read command-line arguments in the process list
Environment variables cannot hold values that come from a secrets vault
Double quotes cause Bash to write the value of the variable to the log
Vault secrets expire when they are passed to any shell script argument

explanation: On most systems the full command line of a running process is visible to other users (for example through ps), so a secret passed as an argument can leak; passing it through an environment variable or a protected file is safer. Environment variables can hold vault values. Quoting does not write values to logs, and secrets do not expire because they are passed as arguments.

prompt: A platform team is reviewing how pipelines handle credentials. Which two practices reduce the risk of secrets being exposed? (Choose two.)

options.text: Printing secret values in the job log at debug level to help troubleshooting
Sharing one administrator credential across all pipelines to simplify rotation
Issuing short-lived credentials to each job instead of long-lived static keys
Fetching secrets from a vault at run time and masking them in job logs
Committing secrets in an encrypted file whose key is stored in the same repository

explanation: Short-lived credentials limit how long a leaked secret is useful, and fetching secrets from a vault at run time with log masking keeps them out of code and output. Encrypting a file while committing its key in the same repository protects nothing. Printing secrets in logs exposes them, and a shared administrator credential gives every pipeline excessive access and a single point of compromise.

prompt: A pipeline runs unit tests on Linux, Windows and macOS one after another, taking 45 minutes in total. The three test runs do not depend on each other. How can the team shorten the pipeline?

options.text: Combine all three runs into one sequential script
Run the three test jobs in parallel
Move the tests after the production deployment step
Run the tests only once a week to save runner time

explanation: Independent jobs can run at the same time on separate runners, so total time drops to roughly the longest single run. One sequential script keeps the same total time. Testing after production deployment defeats the purpose of testing, and weekly runs delay feedback on every change.

prompt: A team's pipeline sometimes deploys code that has not finished testing, because the deploy job starts at the same time as the tests. What should they change?

options.text: Make deploy wait for build and test to succeed, in order
Run deploy in parallel with an extra copy of the tests
Trigger deploy on a timer five minutes after each push to the repository
Remove the test job so that deploy no longer overlaps

explanation: Steps that rely on earlier results must run sequentially, with deploy starting only after build and test pass. A parallel copy of the tests still lets deploy run before they finish. A fixed timer does not guarantee that tests are complete or passed, and removing tests removes the quality gate entirely.

prompt:
A workflow defines the following jobs.

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  test:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  deploy:
    needs: [test, lint]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

(Steps are omitted.) Which jobs start as soon as the workflow is triggered?

options.text: build only
build and lint
build, lint and test
All four jobs at the same time

explanation: Jobs without a needs key have no dependencies and start immediately in parallel, so build and lint begin first. test waits for build, and deploy waits for both test and lint. build is not the only job without dependencies, and neither test nor deploy can start before the jobs they need have succeeded.

prompt:
A pipeline is defined as follows.

stages:
  - build
  - test
  - deploy

compile:
  stage: build
  script: make build
unit-tests:
  stage: test
  script: make test
lint:
  stage: test
  script: make lint
release:
  stage: deploy
  script: make deploy

The unit-tests job fails and lint passes. No other keywords are set. What happens to the release job?

options.text: It runs, because lint passed in the same stage
It runs, because jobs in the deploy stage ignore test stage results
It runs first, because stages execute in reverse order
It does not run, because a job in the test stage failed

explanation: Stages run in the listed order, jobs in the same stage run in parallel, and by default a later stage starts only if every job in the earlier stages succeeded, so a failed unit-tests job stops release. One passing job does not override a failed job in the same stage. Deploy jobs are not exempt from earlier failures, and stages never run in reverse.

prompt: A team wants the deploy job in a workflow to run only for pushes to the main branch, while every other job runs for all branches. Which job-level setting achieves this?

options.text: needs: main
runs-on: main
if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
timeout-minutes: main

explanation: An if condition on the job is evaluated before it runs, and github.ref holds the full ref of the triggering branch, so the job runs only for main. needs lists jobs that must finish first, not branches. runs-on selects the runner, and timeout-minutes sets a time limit and expects a number.

prompt: A job should post an alert to the team's chat channel only when an earlier step in the same job has failed. Which condition should the notification step use?

options.text: if: success()
if: failure()
if: always()
if: cancelled()

explanation: failure() is true when any previous step in the job has failed, so the alert step runs only on failure. success() is the default and runs only when everything before it succeeded. always() runs whatever happens, which would alert on success too, and cancelled() is true only when the workflow was cancelled.

prompt: After each production deployment, the pipeline runs health checks for five minutes. The team wants the previous release restored automatically if the error rate rises above the threshold, without waiting for an engineer. What should the pipeline include?

options.text: A step that redeploys the last known-good version when checks fail
A manual approval gate before every health check is run
A rule that skips health checks during business hours
An email to the release manager asking for a manual rollback decision

explanation: An automated rollback step triggered by failed health checks restores the previous known-good release without human intervention. An approval gate adds a manual delay before checks even run. Skipping checks hides failures, and emailing for a decision is a manual rollback, which is what the team wants to avoid.

prompt: A team plans to add automated rollbacks to its deployment pipeline. Which prerequisite matters most for the rollback to work reliably?

options.text: Every build overwrites the single image tagged latest in the registry
Database schema changes are applied by hand after each release
Earlier versioned artifacts are retained and can be redeployed
The pipeline deletes the previous release once the new one starts

explanation: An automated rollback redeploys a previous release, so earlier artifacts must be kept and identifiable by version. Overwriting one latest tag or deleting the previous release leaves nothing to roll back to. Manual schema changes make the database state unpredictable and can block a clean rollback.

prompt: A pipeline includes a job that checks documentation links. It fails now and then when external sites are slow, but those failures should not block merges. The team still wants to see the result. Which setting handles this in GitLab CI?

options.text: when: never on the link-check job
needs: [] added to every job in the pipeline
stage: .pre on the deploy job
allow_failure: true on the link-check job

explanation: allow_failure: true lets the job fail and be shown with a warning while the pipeline continues and can still pass. when: never stops the job from running, so no result is shown. needs: [] only lets jobs start without waiting for earlier stages, and moving deploy into .pre would run it before everything else.

prompt: A deployment job occasionally hangs on a network call and holds a runner for six hours until the platform's default limit stops it. The job normally completes in eight minutes. What is the best failure-handling change?

options.text: Increase the default timeout so the job has more time to finish
Run the job in parallel with itself so one copy finishes first
Set a job timeout of about 20 minutes so hung runs fail quickly
Disable logging in the job so it uses fewer runner resources

explanation: A timeout slightly above the normal run time ends hung jobs promptly, frees the runner and surfaces the failure. Increasing the timeout makes the problem worse. Running duplicate copies wastes resources and can cause conflicting deployments, and logging has nothing to do with the hang.

prompt: A test matrix runs 12 combinations of language version and operating system. When one combination fails, the other running combinations are cancelled, and developers cannot see which others would also have failed. Which change keeps all combinations running?

options.text: Add needs: [] to the matrix job so it runs independently
Set strategy.fail-fast to false for the matrix
Set continue-on-error to false for each step
Reduce the matrix to a single combination

explanation: In GitHub Actions, matrix jobs default to fail-fast, which cancels in-progress combinations after the first failure; setting fail-fast to false lets them all finish. needs controls dependencies between jobs, not cancellation within a matrix. continue-on-error false is already the default, and shrinking the matrix removes the coverage the team wants.

prompt: A security team wants every pipeline run to flag third-party libraries in the project that have known published vulnerabilities. Which type of scan should be added?

options.text: Software composition analysis (dependency scanning)
Dynamic application security testing against staging
Load testing of the application's busiest endpoint
Code formatting checks on the changed source files

explanation: Software composition analysis compares the project's declared and resolved dependencies with vulnerability databases to find components with known CVEs. Dynamic testing probes a running application's behaviour rather than inventorying its libraries. Load testing measures performance, and formatting checks only look at code style.

prompt: A team wants to catch insecure coding patterns, such as SQL queries built by concatenating user input, by analysing the source code in every pull request without running the application. Which scan should they add?

options.text: Dynamic application security testing (DAST)
A container image vulnerability scan
A synthetic uptime check against production
Static application security testing (SAST)

explanation: SAST analyses source code or bytecode without executing it and flags patterns such as injection risks, which suits pull request checks. DAST needs a running application and tests it from the outside. Container image scanning looks for vulnerable packages in the image, and an uptime check only confirms the service responds.

prompt: A web application is deployed to a staging environment for each release candidate. The security team wants to probe the running application for issues such as missing security headers and injectable input fields. Which scan fits this stage?

options.text: Dynamic application security testing (DAST) against staging
Static analysis of the source code on the developer's laptop
A commit-msg hook that checks the format of commit messages
Software composition analysis of the dependency lock file

explanation: DAST interacts with a running application over HTTP, as an attacker would, so it finds runtime issues such as missing headers and injectable inputs. Static analysis inspects code without running it. A commit-msg hook only validates message text, and composition analysis checks library versions rather than the deployed application's behaviour.

prompt: A pipeline builds a container image from a public base image. The team wants to stop images that contain operating system packages with critical vulnerabilities from reaching the registry. Where should the image scan run?

options.text: After the image has run in production for a week
Before the Dockerfile is written for the service
Only when a customer reports a security incident
After the image is built and before it is pushed

explanation: Scanning the built image before the push step lets the pipeline fail and keep vulnerable images out of the registry. Scanning after a week in production allows the vulnerable image to run in the meantime. There is nothing to scan before the Dockerfile exists, and waiting for a customer report is reactive rather than preventive.

prompt: Builds pass on some CI runners and fail on others because each runner has different versions of the compiler and build tools installed. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Ask the runner administrators to upgrade every tool to the newest release
Run each job inside a pinned container image with the required tools
Retry failed jobs until they happen to land on a working runner
Remove version checks from the build scripts so that any version is accepted

explanation: Running jobs in a container image with pinned tool versions gives every job the same toolchain regardless of which runner picks it up. Upgrading everything to the newest release can break builds and will drift again. Retrying until success hides the inconsistency, and removing version checks allows builds with untested tools.

prompt: A team wants pull requests to be blocked when new code lowers test coverage below 80 percent or adds large amounts of duplicated code. Which pipeline addition provides this?

options.text: A container image scan that runs after each image is pushed
A webhook that posts the coverage number to a chat channel
A code quality scan with an enforced quality gate
A nightly load test that measures response times in staging

explanation: Code quality tools measure coverage, duplication and complexity, and a quality gate with thresholds fails the pipeline when they are not met, which blocks the merge. Image scanning finds vulnerable packages, not coverage problems. A chat notification reports the number without enforcing anything, and load tests measure performance.

prompt: A platform team receives hundreds of failed pipeline runs a week and wants to use an AI-based log analysis tool. Which use of the tool is most appropriate?

options.text: Automatically merge any code change the tool predicts will fix the failure
Replace all pipeline test steps, because the tool can predict failures
Cluster similar failures and flag likely causes for an engineer to verify
Delete logs that the tool classifies as unimportant without retaining them

explanation: AI log analysis is useful for clustering recurring failures, surfacing anomalous lines and suggesting likely causes, with a human verifying the conclusion. Automatically merging predicted fixes skips review and can introduce new defects. Predictions do not replace actual tests, and deleting logs based on a model's judgement can destroy evidence needed later.

prompt: A team plans to send its CI job logs to an external AI service for automated failure analysis. What should be done before enabling this?

options.text: Increase the log level to DEBUG so the service receives more detail
Redact secrets and personal data from the logs before they are sent
Disable secret masking so the service can see the actual values
Send only the logs from successful runs so failures stay private

explanation: CI logs can contain tokens, internal host names and personal data, so they should be scrubbed and the data handling reviewed before they leave the organisation. Raising the log level increases the amount of sensitive detail. Disabling masking exposes secrets directly, and sending only successful runs defeats the purpose of analysing failures.

prompt: A CI server checks the Git repository for changes every 15 minutes, so builds often start long after a push. The team wants builds to start within seconds of each push. What should they configure?

options.text: A shorter polling interval of one minute configured on the CI server
A nightly scheduled pipeline that builds all recent commits
A manual trigger that developers click after every push
A webhook on the Git host that notifies the CI server of each push

explanation: With a webhook, the Git host sends an HTTP request to the CI server as soon as the push event happens, so builds start almost immediately. Polling every minute still adds delay and creates constant load on the Git server. A nightly schedule delays builds by hours, and manual clicks depend on people remembering to do it.

prompt: A CI server exposes a public endpoint that receives push webhooks and starts deployments. The team is worried that anyone who discovers the URL could send fake events. What is the standard protection?

options.text: Validate each request against a shared webhook secret
Change the endpoint URL every week and email it to the team
Accept webhook requests only when they arrive with the GET method
Log every webhook payload and review the log once a month

explanation: Git hosts let a shared secret be configured for each webhook, either to sign the payload with an HMAC or to send as a token header, and the receiver checks it to reject forged requests. Rotating a secret URL is obscurity, not authentication. Push webhooks are delivered with POST, so a GET-only rule would reject genuine events without adding security, and a monthly log review detects abuse far too late.

prompt: An operations team wants engineers to start deployments and check pipeline status by typing commands in the team's chat channel, with every action visible to the rest of the team. Which practice is this?

options.text: ChatOps, using a chat bot connected to the CI/CD system
Pair programming, using a shared screen during deployments
Polling, using a script that checks the chat history nightly
Blue-green deployment, using two chat rooms for releases

explanation: ChatOps connects chat tools to automation through a bot, so commands such as deploy or status run from the channel and the results are visible to everyone there. Pair programming is two people working on code together. A nightly script reading chat history is not interactive automation, and blue-green is a release strategy, not a chat practice.

prompt: A team has set up a chat bot that can deploy to production when someone types /deploy prod. Security reviewers are concerned about this ChatOps setup. Which control is most important to add?

options.text: Let anyone in the chat workspace deploy, to encourage collaboration
Have the bot use a senior engineer's personal credentials
Check that the requesting user is authorised for production deploys
Delete the chat history after each deployment for privacy

explanation: The bot must check that the person issuing the command is allowed to perform that action, and record who did what, because chat membership alone is not authorisation. Allowing everyone to deploy removes access control. Personal credentials tie automation to one person and grant their full rights, and deleting history removes the audit trail that makes ChatOps valuable.

prompt:
A workflow file contains the following trigger.

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
      - 'release/**'

A developer pushes to four branches. Which push does NOT start the workflow?

options.text: A push to main
A push to release/2.4
A push to release/2.4/hotfix
A push to feature/login

explanation: The branch filter lists main and the pattern release/**, where ** matches any characters including slashes, so main, release/2.4 and release/2.4/hotfix all match. feature/login matches neither entry, so pushing to it does not trigger the workflow.

prompt: A team wants its release workflow to run only when a version tag such as v2.1.0 is pushed, and not on ordinary branch pushes. Which trigger configuration does this?

options.text: on: push: branches: ['v*.*.*']
on: push: tags: ['v*.*.*']
on: pull_request: branches: [main]
on: schedule: - cron: 'v*.*.*'

explanation: A push trigger with a tags filter runs only when a matching tag is pushed, and with only a tags filter, branch pushes do not trigger it. A branches filter with the same pattern matches branch names, not tags. A pull_request trigger fires on pull request activity, and a cron expression must contain schedule fields, not a tag pattern.

prompt: An operator wants to start a deployment workflow by hand from the CI web interface and choose the target environment from a list each time. Which trigger configuration supports this?

options.text: on: push with a branches filter set to the environment names
on: schedule with a cron expression for each environment
on: workflow_dispatch with an input listing the environments
on: pull_request with a types filter set to opened

explanation: workflow_dispatch adds a manual run option to the workflow, and its inputs can define a choice of environments that the operator selects at run time. A push trigger runs automatically when code is pushed. A schedule runs on a timer, and pull_request runs when pull requests change, none of which is a manual choice.

prompt: In a GitLab CI pipeline, the production deploy job must appear in every pipeline on main but must not start until a person clicks to run it. Which keyword should be added to the job?

options.text: when: always
allow_failure: true
retry: 2
when: manual

explanation: when: manual makes the job wait in the pipeline until a user starts it, giving a manual gate before production. when: always runs the job automatically whatever the earlier results. allow_failure lets a failed job not block the pipeline, and retry reruns a job automatically after a failure.

prompt: A declarative Jenkinsfile must pause before the production stage until an authorised person approves the deployment in the Jenkins interface. Which step should be used?

options.text: input with a message such as 'Deploy to production?'
sh 'sleep 3600' so someone has an hour to cancel
parallel to run the approval and the deploy together
retry(3) so the stage is attempted three times

explanation: The input step pauses the pipeline and waits for a user to approve or abort, and it can be limited to specific submitters. Sleeping for an hour does not ask for approval and continues automatically. Running approval and deployment in parallel lets the deploy happen without waiting, and retry repeats a failed block rather than waiting for approval.

prompt:
A workflow includes the following trigger. Scheduled workflows on this platform use UTC.

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 2 * * 1-5'

When does the workflow run?

options.text: Every two hours on weekdays
At 02:00 UTC, Monday through Friday
At 00:02 UTC every day of the week
At 02:00 UTC on the 1st to 5th of each month

explanation: The five cron fields are minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week, so 0 2 * * 1-5 means minute 0 of hour 2 on days of the week 1 to 5 (Monday to Friday). Every two hours would need */2 in the hour field. Reading the fields in the wrong order gives 00:02, and 1-5 in the fifth field is the day of week, not the day of the month.

prompt: A GitLab project runs a nightly scheduled pipeline. The team wants a long-running dependency audit job to run only in that scheduled pipeline, not in pipelines started by pushes. Which rule should the job use?

options.text: rules: - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "schedule"
rules: - if: $CI_COMMIT_TAG == "nightly"
rules: - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "schedule"
rules: - when: manual

explanation: CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE records how the pipeline was started and equals schedule for scheduled pipelines, so the rule limits the job to them. CI_COMMIT_BRANCH holds a branch name, not the trigger type. CI_COMMIT_TAG is set only in tag pipelines, and when: manual requires someone to start the job in every pipeline.

prompt: A GitLab CI job builds a container image, and every image must be traceable to the exact commit it was built from. Which tag should the job apply?

options.text: $CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA
$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE
$CI_JOB_STATUS
latest

explanation: CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA holds the abbreviated hash of the commit being built, so it links each image to its source revision. CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE only says how the pipeline started, such as push or schedule. CI_JOB_STATUS reports whether the job succeeded or failed, and latest is a moving tag that does not identify a commit.

prompt: A GitLab job should publish a release only when a Git tag is pushed, using the tag name as the version number. Which configuration fits?

options.text: rules: - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main", then use $CI_COMMIT_SHA
rules: - if: $CI_COMMIT_TAG, then use $CI_COMMIT_TAG in the script
rules: - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "web", then use $CI_JOB_ID
rules: - when: always, then use the literal text latest as the version
